description:
Earthlight FM is a creative take on the Earth Information Jukebox: turning NASA's views of our planet at night into sound, with a strong focus on design and accessibility.

I'm Aya, a senior CS student and web developer from Lebanon, building this project solo for NASA Space Apps 2026.

Made for those who can't see, and beautiful for those who can. Every light is a person, a home, a sound, proof that we were here, and still are.
summary:
Earthlight FM is a web-based Earth Jukebox that turns NASA's Black Marble night lights into music, so anyone, including blind and low-vision people, can experience how our planet changed between 2012 and 2023.

Users pick a continent and a time: the 2012 to 2023 change map, a single year, or two years to compare. The app reads NASA's Earth Information Center frames pixel by pixel in real time and plays the region from west to east. A kalimba plays where light grew, a stylophone plays where it faded, and silence means no real change. Every note comes from the data, on a pentatonic scale so it stays musical.

A retro control room shows the same story visually: a turning globe, a brightness graph, a live waveform and notes. A field report printer explains each melody in plain text.

Night lights are people, homes and cities. Earthlight FM makes that change something you can hear, not only see.
details:
What it does

Earthlight FM pairs NASA Earth Information Center visual frames with sound generated in real time. The user chooses a region on a world map and a time period, presses play, and hears the night lights of that region as a melody.

How it works

1. NASA's night lights images (SVS 5313 / 5276) are loaded into an HTML canvas and read pixel by pixel in the browser.

2. The selected region, defined as a latitude/longitude box, is cut into 32 vertical slices, read west to east, one beat per slice. Empty ocean at the edges is skipped.

3. What changed (2012 to 2023): purple pixels (more light) play a kalimba, orange pixels (less light) play a stylophone. A stronger change plays a higher, louder note.

4. One year: brighter lights play higher, louder notes, measured on the same scale as 2023 so years can be compared.

5. Two years: each slice is measured by its own percentage change; changes under 5% are treated as sensor noise and stay silent.

6. All notes use a pentatonic scale, so the data stays musical instead of chaotic.

Benefits and impact

NASA's Earth visualizations are powerful but only visual. Earthlight FM gives blind and low-vision people a way to explore Earth data through sound and gives everyone an emotional connection to the data: every light is a person, a home, a sound.

Accessibility

Controls are real buttons usable with the keyboard, the map can be navigated with Tab and Enter, live text tells screen readers what is playing, and the printed field report explains each melody in words. Colors are always paired with text labels. Next steps: testing with screen-reader users and blind listeners.

Creativity

The interface is a retro broadcast control room: a turning globe, brightness graph, live waveform, flowing notes, a system log, and a printer that prints a data-driven field report. The kalimba (organic, warm) and stylophone (electronic, buzzy) were chosen to represent growth and loss of light.

Tools

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Tone.js (sound synthesis), HTML Canvas (pixel analysis), GitHub Pages (hosting), Clipchamp (demo video).

Considerations and limits

Regions are approximate rectangles, satellite readings vary slightly year to year (clouds, moonlight, sensor changes, LED street lights), and changes under 5% are ignored to avoid false notes.

Use of AI

As a solo participant, I used Claude (an AI assistant) for explaining new tools, generating and refining code, debugging, and editing text. The concept, design, art direction and sound identity are my own, and I reviewed and tested every part of the code.
